results.title: Why do kde estimates from ks and adehabitatHR packages in R produce different results? (with same bandwidth and grid)
results.content: # Why do kde estimates from ks and adehabitatHR packages in R produce different results? The first function relies entirely on the ks package, by using the kde() function and a pre-defined grid expanded by a factor of the bandwidth to get the volume of the Utilization distribution (UD). grid.vol <- sum(cell.area\*output[,3]) #check that grid UD vol is >=0.99. KDE <- data.frame(c(area,grid.vol)). This code transforms the bandwidth and kde from the ks package with rasters to utilize functions in the adehabitatHR function to easily get UD volumes and areas. The difference between my code and the one in the book is that I define the grid using the same methods as the first function. y.expand <- band.mult\*sqrt(data.h[2,2]) #set the value used to expand the grid by a function of the multiplier and the bandwidth. x.expand <- band.mult\*sqrt(data.h[1,1]) #note that this expansion is different in the x and y direction. Not really that big a difference from the other value of 3958 m^2- but I would love to know where it comes from, as it the difference between the two functions can vary based on how I define the grid, multiplier, or percentage. I don't use the KDE and UD functions in R much, but I can see two possible reasons for the discrepencies. The first is due to the extent used to calculate the KDEs/UDs. As these are based on a grid structure, if you process the same data with different extents (that is different coordinates for the four corners of the grid that is generated), you cna get slightly different resutls. Different tools can use different default functions for this smoothing process (such as Gausian or quadratic) and this can result in different density estimates for specific grid cells for the outputs. You are right about the extent and the function being two obvious reasons for why kde estimates could be different. Notably, in the second method, I did not use that functions default method of defining the bandwidth and instead used the ks package to define the bandwidth with the plug-in method in both cases.

results.title: Optimizing vessel trajectories: Advanced denoising and interpolation techniques for AIS data - ScienceDirect
results.content: # Research paper Optimizing vessel trajectories: Advanced denoising and interpolation techniques for AIS data. Developed a comprehensive framework for denoising and interpolating AIS data to enhance trajectory quality. Utilized kinematic-based interpolation for short gaps and historical data transfer for long gaps to restore trajectories. The quality of vessel trajectory data is essential for effective maritime traffic control, enhanced situational awareness, and the advancement of maritime algorithms. This study introduces a comprehensive framework for AIS trajectory denoising and interpolation, aimed at restoring incomplete and noisy vessel trajectories. Significant progress has been made in the field of vessel trajectory reconstruction, particularly in trajectory denoising and interpolation techniques (Chen et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2018). This paper aims to investigate vessel trajectory reconstruction methods based on AIS data, exploring ways to enhance the reliability and accuracy of trajectory data in the presence of noise and data gaps, thereby providing robust support for maritime safety and navigation.

results.title: comparison of VMS and AIS data: the effect of data coverage and vessel position recording frequency on estimates of fishing footprints | ICES Journal of Marine Science | Oxford Academic
results.content: Jennifer L Shepperson, Niels T Hintzen, Claire L Szostek, Ewen Bell, Lee G Murray, Michel J Kaiser, A comparison of VMS and AIS data: the effect of data coverage and vessel position recording frequency on estimates of fishing footprints, *ICES Journal of Marine Science*, Volume 75, Issue 3, May-June 2018, Pages 988–998,. VMS and AIS data were compared for individual scallop fishing vessels. Besides the lower overall fleet coverage of AIS data (i.e. number of vessels with AIS), it would be useful to understand more about the differences in inferred fishing activity between VMS and AIS data, where the coverage is concurrent. The main aims of this article were to: (i) determine the relative coverage of AIS data in relation to VMS data at both the fleet and an individual vessel level; and (ii) for matching data (from the same vessels in the same time period), determine whether the fishing extent and intensity predicted by three common methods of VMS data analysis point density, straight line (SL) interpolation ([Stelzenmuller *et al.* 2008), and cubic Hermite spline (cHs) interpolation (Hintzen *et al.* 2010)] showed a comparable accuracy to the higher poll frequency AIS data. The time spent fishing and area swept columns indicate the total for each vessel using comparable and matching VMS and AIS data. The time spent fishing and area swept columns indicate the total for each vessel using comparable and matching VMS and AIS data. The estimates of fishing extent presented here are not absolute efforts of scallop dredging activity in the English Channel, as data were only available from eight vessels, and only subsections of data which are temporally matched between AIS and VMS data were used. The cHs interpolation of the VMS data at 1-km cell resolution gave a very similar value for the extent of fishing as the SL AIS at 1-km cell resolution, but the point VMS data at 1-km cell resolution greatly underestimated the extent of fishing activity. When VMS and AIS data were directly matching in temporal coverage, the scale of analysis (i.e. size of the grid cells) had the greatest influence on the estimates of fishing extent and intensity compared with the data-type (AIS, VMS) and data treatment (point, SL, cHs).
